provisions_triggered.name: Due Process / Law of the Land

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Due Process Clause requires a State to support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence before it may permanently terminate parental rights, and that intermediate standard — rather than proof beyond a reasonable doubt — satisfies due process.
key_cases.relevance: Supplies the federal constitutional floor that Alaska implements through AS 47.10.088 and CINA Rule 18(c), which require clear and convincing evidence of the statutory termination grounds.
key_cases.quote: We hold that such a standard adequately conveys to the factfinder the level of subjective certainty about his factual conclusions necessary to satisfy due process.

key_cases.case_name: Christopher C. v. State, Department of Health & Social Services, Office of Children's Services
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed termination of parental rights to Indian children, holding that failure to remedy and active efforts must be proved by clear and convincing evidence, that best interests is found by a preponderance, and that placement objections — including cultural ones — belong in a placement review, not the termination trial.
key_cases.relevance: States Alaska's layered termination standard: clear and convincing evidence on the grounds, preponderance on best interests.
key_cases.quote: Challenges to placement decisions, including challenges based on cultural concerns, are not properly raised in a termination proceeding.

key_cases.case_name: Demetria H. v. State, Department of Health & Social Services, Office of Children's Services
key_cases.holding: An ICWA qualified expert witness need not have met the child or family so long as the court has sufficient information about the family's particular circumstances, and the court may aggregate expert and lay testimony to support the serious-harm finding.
key_cases.relevance: Controls the qualified-expert-witness element of the beyond-a-reasonable-doubt serious-harm finding required to terminate rights to an Indian child.
key_cases.quote: The trial court did not err in qualifying Kaufman as an expert witness or using his testimony to support its substantial risk of harm finding.

key_cases.case_name: Native Village of Tununak v. State, Department of Health & Social Services, Office of Children's Services
key_cases.holding: Overruling its prior application of Adoption Rule 11's preponderance standard, the court held that good cause to deviate from ICWA's adoptive placement preferences must be proved by clear and convincing evidence, and vacated and remanded for application of that standard.
key_cases.relevance: Governs the placement determination that accompanies adoption after termination of parental rights.
key_cases.quote: we conclude that ICWA implicitly mandates that good cause to deviate from ICWA's adoptive placement preferences be proved by clear and convincing evidence

key_cases.case_name: Penn P. v. State, Department of Health & Social Services, Office of Children's Services
key_cases.holding: Termination was affirmed: the superior court's reliance on unadmitted drug-treatment records was harmless, and the father failed to overcome the presumption that counsel's decision not to object was tactical, so he did not show ineffective assistance.
key_cases.relevance: Sets the standard a parent must meet to upset a termination order on evidentiary or ineffective-assistance grounds.
key_cases.quote: We affirm the termination order because relying on the unadmitted drug-treatment records was harmless error and because the father has not shown that he received ineffective assistance of counsel.

key_cases.case_name: Alex H. v. State, Department of Health & Social Services, Office of Children's Services
key_cases.holding: An incarcerated parent who participated telephonically in his termination trial was not denied due process when the superior court declined to order his transport, because he showed no way his in-person presence would have reduced the risk of an erroneous result.
key_cases.relevance: Controls whether an incarcerated Alaska parent may insist on physical presence at a termination trial.
key_cases.quote: The superior court did not violate Alex's right to due process by declining to order his transport.

key_cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Services of Durham County
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: Due process does not require appointment of counsel for an indigent parent in every parental termination proceeding; the trial court decides case by case under the Mathews v. Eldridge factors against a presumption that appointed counsel is required only where physical liberty is at stake, and the refusal to appoint counsel here was not error.
key_cases.relevance: Is the federal companion to Santosky on termination procedure: it sets the constitutional floor for appointed counsel, which Alaska exceeds by statute, so an Alaska practitioner must cite both.
key_cases.quote: neither can we say that the Constitution requires the appointment of counsel in every parental termination proceeding

extended_foster_care_age: To the 21st birthday by court order only: state custody ends at the 19th birthday unless the court grants one-year extensions past 19, which require the person's consent and a best-interests finding, and a person already released from care may ask the court to resume custody before the 21st birthday (Alaska Stat. § 47.10.080(c)(1)(B), § 47.10.080(v), § 47.10.100(a))

common_failures: Failure to prove unfitness by clear and convincing evidence
Santosky v. Kramer standard not met

timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Must file TPR or document compelling reason
